hook: Fires across Brazil's Amazonas state surged 253 percent in October 2026.

sections.voiceover: Fires across Brazil's Amazonas state surged 253 percent in October 2026.
sections.visual_cue: Aerial view of smoke plumes rising from dense Amazon rainforest canopy

b_roll: Satellite view of fire hotspots in South America

sections.voiceover: Brazil's surveillance system recorded 1,679 fires in Amazonas state during early October. Why did thick smoke engulf Manaus?
sections.visual_cue: Map highlighting Amazonas state shifting to a satellite view over Manaus shrouded in haze
b_roll: Manaus city skyline covered in heavy smoke

sections.voiceover: But Scientific American reported the Amazon hasn't recovered from drought linked to El Niño in 2023.
sections.visual_cue: Archival footage of charred tree trunks from previous drought seasons
b_roll: Dry cracked soil in rainforest riverbed

sections.voiceover: El Niño dried out rainforest vegetation, creating extreme fire risks. That 253 percent fire surge pushed the ecosystem toward a tipping point.
sections.visual_cue: Split visual showing dried-up river margins and active fire lines spreading through dry brush
sections.sfx_cue: Deep bass hit followed by wind noise
b_roll: Low Amazon river water levels expose mudbanks

sections.voiceover: Scientific American reported in November 2026 that the Amazon hasn't recovered from past droughts.

b_roll: Sunset over Amazon river basin with lingering smoke
